name: Omar Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission maintenance crew, so the big steel towers that carry power across the moors, not the little poles in the street. A normal day starts at six at the Kettle Moor yard, then a long drive on farm tracks, then climbing a tower to change insulators or fix a damper that's worked loose. On a clear day you can see three counties from the top, and I still love that after twenty-two years. What wears me out is the waiting: for the outage permit, for the weather, for someone in an office to say yes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Twenty-two years. What did you do before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All sorts. Kitchens, then a few years driving lorries, then I got the apprenticeship at thirty-six, which was late. I've always liked trying new things. That's also how I lost our savings, but we'll get to that, I'm sure.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mira and I ran a food van on weekends, five years ago. Great food, terrible location, and we're still paying off the loan for the van. So we've got about three weeks of money in the bank, and our two kids are grown and gone. Our region's grade is lower pay than the city crews, and the nearest other tower work is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly. I use these AI tools every day, to read through the drone inspection reports and to study, and I was looking forward to them getting better. I'd probably post something like, shame, I wanted a smarter apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing much changes, which isn't bad. I'd still get my pension at sixty-six if I keep climbing. The problem is the van loan and the low grade, and those are there with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at what I'm doing, and I'd keep using the tools for the boring bits, like writing up defects and checking the torque tables. I'd put in for the drone pilot course the company runs, because they'll want more of those either way. Maybe I'd look at whether that comes with a higher grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bit bored, if that's allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How exactly do you use the AI tools at work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This morning I took a photo of a corroded clamp on tower 41 and asked it what I was looking at and what the standard says. It gave me the right answer and the page number, which saved a call to the engineer. My crew think I'm mad, but they ask me to do it for them now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the van lost you money. Does that make you more careful now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With money, yes. With learning, no. Learning something new costs me evenings, not savings, so I'll always do that.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, because I use AI tools every day and wanted them to get better. I'd post something like, shame, I wanted a smarter apprentice.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for me, which isn't bad, since I'd still reach my pension at sixty-six. My real problems are the van loan and the low regional grade.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI tools for defect write-ups and torque tables. Puts in for the company's drone pilot course and asks whether it comes with a higher grade.
S0.quote: Learning something new costs me evenings, not savings, so I'll always do that.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is the only one on his crew who uses AI daily, and his colleagues now come to him for it. A failed food van has made him careful with money but not with learning. He sees the drone course as a route to better pay whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the union earns its money. The tools are coming, so let's make sure we're the ones trained to run them, and that the savings show up in our pay. I'd say that loudly at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out of this all right. Drones are already doing the inspection walks, and someone has to fly them, read the data and fix what they find. If I've got the pilot licence and I'm good with the software, I'm the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the drone licence and ask to move onto the inspection team, even if it means more driving. I'd use the AI tools to help me learn the thermal camera stuff, the heat pictures that show a failing joint. And I'd push the branch to get every older climber offered the same course, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Curious, a bit excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, mainly. He's fifty-nine and the best climber I've ever seen, but he won't touch a phone if he can avoid it. I've offered to teach him, and he says he'll retire before he learns to swipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd lose in that move to inspection work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The view, and the climbing. Flying a drone from the back of a van isn't the same as standing on the top arm of a tower in the wind. I'd miss that more than I'd admit to Mira.

S1.say: I'd say this is where the union earns its money, by making sure workers are trained to run the new tools and share in the savings. I'd say it loudly at work and online.
S1.think: I think I'd come out of this all right, because drones already do inspection and someone has to fly them and read the data. If I have the licence and the software skills, I'm the one they keep.
S1.do: Finishes the drone licence in the first year and asks to move to the inspection team. Uses AI tools to learn thermal camera work and pushes the union branch to offer the course to every older climber.
S1.feel: Curious and a bit excited, with some sadness about leaving the climbing.
S1.quote: Flying a drone from the back of a van isn't the same as standing on the top arm of a tower in the wind.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like an opening for Omar, not a threat, because he's already halfway there. He pairs his own move with a union push so older colleagues aren't left out. The only loss he names is the joy of the climb itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong public support. If machines can do nearly all the work, the gains have to be shared, through tax and something like a basic income. I'd be campaigning for that, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years is too fast even for me. I'd be sixty, with three weeks of savings and a van loan, and if robots can climb towers and drones read them, my drone licence buys me maybe a year. I like change, but I like it when I can steer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the drone and robot side the first week, whatever courses there are, and ask to help test the robots on our lines, because the people who test them get kept on longest. We'd sell the van for whatever we can get and put the money against the loan. And I'd join whatever campaign is pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but my stomach would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to build anything. With more time I could get the licence, get the inspection job, save a bit, and roll into retirement. With two, I'm grabbing at whatever's floating past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we sell the van this month and stop pretending we'll ever use it again. She'd be upset, it was her dream more than mine. But she'd agree, she's more sensible than me.

S2.say: I'd say this is why we need strong public support, sharing the gains through tax and something like a basic income. I'd campaign for that without question.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for me: I'd be sixty with three weeks of savings and a loan, and a drone licence might buy me a year. I like change when I can steer it.
S2.do: Signs up for drone and robot courses in the first week and volunteers to help test robots on his lines. Sells the food van to pay down the loan and joins a basic income campaign.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight stomach, but not frozen.
S2.quote: I like change, but I like it when I can steer it.
S2.fieldNote: Even an adaptive person like Omar hits a wall when the timeline leaves no room to build. His instinct is still to move first, by volunteering to test the robots. Selling the van is a quiet admission that one dream has ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, louder: we've got five years, so build the safety net now. Training for everyone, a share of the gains, and a plan for the people the machines replace. I'd be out campaigning for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three, and that's a decent run. I could get the licence, move to inspection, maybe even help run the robots, and still have a few years of income before it all changes. I think I'd be all right, with some luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, the drone licence and the move to inspection. Year two, whatever robot operator course appears, and I'd use the AI tools every evening to study for it. Mira and I would clear the van loan and start saving properly, and I'd offer to teach the crew the basics on weekends, maybe for a bit of extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the extra three years change the way you'd think about retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They do. With five years I might even work past sixty-six, if the work is flying drones and not climbing. I'd want to choose when I stop, not have it chosen for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach the crew. Would they want that from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. Gary wouldn't, but the younger lads already ask me how I do things on my phone. I'd do it at the yard on Saturday mornings with tea and bacon rolls, and charge the company, not them.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so build the safety net now with training, a share of the gains and a plan for those replaced. I'd be out campaigning for it.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, with time to get the licence, move to inspection and maybe run the robots. With some luck I think I'd be all right.
S3.do: Gets the drone licence and moves to inspection in year one, then takes a robot operator course in year two while studying with AI tools. Clears the van loan, starts saving and offers paid weekend training sessions to his crew.
S3.feel: Slightly uneasy but more excited than scared.
S3.quote: I'd do it at the yard on Saturday mornings with tea and bacon rolls, and charge the company, not them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Omar's mood around, because it's enough time to build a path step by step. He even talks about working past sixty-six on his own terms. His teaching plan mixes generosity to his crew with a sharp eye for getting paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade's enough to do it properly, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. I'd say the union and the government should start planning tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd be sixty-eight and either retired or doing some drone work part-time because I enjoy it. My worry would be for my kids, who'd be in their forties when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone licence and the inspection move, same as before, but without the panic. I'd clear the loan, put a bit by each month, and help the branch set up training for younger members. I'd also tell my son, who's a plumber, to start learning the smart heating systems now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been confident across these. Is there anything that would knock that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, honestly. Everything I've said assumes my body holds out to sixty-six. If it doesn't, all the courses in the world won't matter, and three weeks of savings won't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather have the ten years or the two, if you could choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten, without a doubt. Part of me likes the idea of a big shake-up, but not when I'm sixty with a van loan.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is enough to do it properly, so nobody should be left behind. The union and the government should start planning tomorrow.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight, retired or doing drone work part-time for the enjoyment. My worry would be for my kids, who'd be in their forties when it lands.
S4.do: Takes the drone licence and inspection move calmly, clears the loan and saves a little each month. Helps the union branch set up training for younger members and tells his plumber son to learn smart heating systems.
S4.quote: Everything I've said assumes my body holds out to sixty-six.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Omar is calm and thinking about his children. The one thing that shakes him is his own body, not the technology. He prefers the slow path despite enjoying change, which says a lot about his money position.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is training paid for and on work time, for older workers too, and some kind of basic income so a sixty-year-old isn't choosing between a course and the gas bill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'm scared of the AI itself. I'm not, I talk to it every day. I'm scared of who owns it.

headlineQuote: I'm not, I talk to it every day. I'm scared of who owns it.
portrait: Omar Olsen is a fifty-eight-year-old transmission lineworker who climbs steel towers across the moors on a lower regional pay grade. He uses AI tools every day, studies in the evenings and is chasing a drone pilot licence, but a failed food van left him and his partner with a loan and about three weeks of savings. He backs unions, public support and a basic income, and worries about who owns the technology rather than the technology itself. He is calm in the mild pictures, anxious only when AGI arrives in two years, and more upbeat as warning time grows because he can build a path step by step.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years leaves no time to build a path at sixty with a loan and little savings.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training on work time for older workers, and a basic income so people don't have to choose between a course and the gas bill.
